claims.text: Phase stability in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys is governed by the development of chemical short-range order during controlled thermal treatments.
Preferential atomic interactions occur between Al and transition metals such as Cr and Fe.
These preferential interactions promote local B2-like ordering within the solid-solution matrix.
Chemical short-range order reduces local lattice distortions.
Chemical short-range order limits defect mobility.
The as-cast, homogenized baseline has a nominally random elemental distribution.
Equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys typically have an FCC or dual-phase structure in the stated initial condition.
Annealing at 800–1000 °C for 1–24 hours followed by controlled cooling can produce varying degrees of chemical short-range order.
The ordered clusters formed by the treatment predominantly involve Al and selected transition-metal atoms.
Short-range-ordered clusters are energetically favorable.
Short-range order inhibits defect migration.
Short-range order inhibits defect coalescence.
Stabilization by short-range order mitigates phase separation.
Stabilization by short-range order suppresses the formation of deleterious secondary phases.
Samples with more short-range order will develop fewer secondary phases after high-temperature and irradiation exposures than the near-random baseline.
Samples with more short-range order will accumulate fewer defects after high-temperature and irradiation exposures than the near-random baseline.
Samples with more short-range order will have higher high-temperature yield strength than the near-random baseline.
Samples with more short-range order will have greater cryogenic toughness than the near-random baseline.
The short-range-order-stabilized microstructure supports environmental resistance.
The short-range-order-stabilized microstructure supports radiation tolerance.
